object.help: A previous run whose output becomes this run's identity and palette. How a character sheet feeds an animation without regenerating the character.
object.label: Inherit from run

object.help: How hard style references push. Deliberately an order of magnitude below identity — at identity strength a style exemplar replaces your character with the exemplar.
object.label: Style exemplar strength

object.help: A reference within this many degrees of the frame's viewing angle counts as a match and gets full weight.
object.label: Match tolerance

object.help: Find per-view references by filename instead of listing them, so a job can be written by a script and queued in bulk with nothing uploaded. Template over {name} (or {id}) and {view}, e.g. overnight/{name}/refs/{view}.png. Views: front, back, side_left, side_right. Only files that exist are added, and a view you configured explicitly always wins.
object.label: Reference path pattern

object.help: What covers a side with no reference of its own. 'mirror' reuses the other side flipped - right for a symmetric outfit, wrong for a cape or an asymmetric skirt. 'back' shares most silhouette with a profile. 'none' leaves pick() to weaken the nearest reference, which is the honest default when nothing is known.
object.label: Missing side

object.help: IP-Adapter weight when a reference matches the view. High is correct here — you have real evidence of what that side looks like.
object.label: Weight when matched

object.help: Weight at a full 180-degree mismatch, interpolated in between. Keep this LOW. Forcing a front reference onto a rear generation produces a front-facing sprite that fights the pose; a weak hint leaves the model free to invent the unseen side.
object.label: Weight when unmatched

object.help: On: weight is chosen per frame from angular distance. Off: the fixed Identity weight is used for every frame.
object.label: Automatic falloff

object.help: dpmpp_2m is the SDXL workhorse. dpmpp_3m_sde and uni_pc cost more per step and can resolve finer detail. Must be 'lcm' when LCM mode is on.
object.label: Sampler

object.help: karras concentrates steps where they matter most. sgm_uniform is required by LCM.
object.label: Scheduler

object.help: Must be 'lcm' when Fast LCM mode is on — LCM is a distilled model and an ordinary sampler will not converge inside its step budget. Off LCM, dpmpp_2m as on the anchor.
object.label: Sampler (frames)

object.help: sgm_uniform under LCM, karras otherwise, matching the anchor. The scheduler decides where the steps are spent, and LCM's distillation assumes the uniform spacing.
object.label: Scheduler (frames)

object.help: Send the pose guide and depth map to the anchor as well as to the frames. Without it the anchor is generated from prompt and reference alone, which is how a bow ended up drawn twice: the words said 'holding a bow' and nothing said where. With it too strong the anchor traces the depth silhouette instead. The strengths below default lower than the frames stage's because the anchor has no anchor of its own to pull against.
object.label: Condition the anchor

object.help: 0 disables the pose channel without disabling depth.
object.label: Anchor pose strength

object.help: Fraction of sampling the control steers for. Held late, the model draws the guide rather than a character.
object.label: Anchor control end

object.help: How long one image may take before the run gives up. Per image, not per stage — candidates are generated sequentially, so four of them get four separate budgets.
object.label: Timeout (seconds)

object.help: Per frame. A stage that hangs holds the queue, so this is the difference between one bad job and a wasted night.
object.label: Timeout (seconds)

object.help: Generate this many canonical sprites in one batch and keep them all, so you can pick the best identity anchor instead of re-rolling. Batching amortises the ~35s fixed cost per prompt.
object.label: Canonical candidates

object.help: Also grows the skull in the depth map, which is where head volume actually reads.
object.label: Head size

object.help: 1.0 is the rig's default. 2.0 gives a giraffe-like or serpentine neck.
object.label: Neck length

object.help: Stretches the spine; the limbs follow their anchors.
object.label: Torso length

object.help: Long-armed apes, short-armed brawlers.
object.label: Arm length

object.help: Below 1.0 gives a stubby, chibi stance.
object.label: Leg length

object.help: Ignored by rigs with no tail.
object.label: Tail length

object.help: Ignored by rigs with no wings.
object.label: Wing span

object.help: Octopoid rigs only.
object.label: Tentacle length

object.help: Serpent and centipede rigs only.
object.label: Segment length

object.help: Off by default for a character sheet, on for an animation, and the same prop list serves both. A sheet is a reference document - a weapon occludes the torso and arm it crosses, and is a long rigid volume the model will trace instead of the limb behind it. An attack animation is the opposite: without the weapon the arm swings at nothing.
object.label: Draw held objects

object.help: Base diffusion weights. SDXL is what the pixel LoRA was trained against; swapping the base usually means swapping the LoRA too.
object.label: Checkpoint

object.help: The LoRA that makes the output read as pixel art rather than a downscaled painting. Every other default here is tuned around it, so swapping it means re-tuning both lora_strength dials.
object.label: Style LoRA

object.help: Apply the canonical sprite to every frame at equal weight, underneath the matched identity reference. It is the only input that does not vary, so it is what keeps frames on-model with each other. Turning it off reverts to steering from the reference alone, which leaves rear views with no anchor.
object.label: Anchor to canonical

object.help: How hard the canonical pulls. Too high and every frame becomes the canonical's pose; too low and the frames drift apart.
object.label: Anchor weight

object.help: What the anchor carries. Keep 'linear'. 'style and composition' also copies the canonical's LAYOUT, and the canonical is front-facing — at anchor weight 0.9 it outvoted the depth map that carries yaw and every side and rear frame came back facing front, with the canonical's backdrop over the keyed one.
object.label: Anchor transfer

object.help: How much the anchor weakens as a frame turns away from it. Reference weight already falls off with angle; the anchor's did not, so on a rear frame the FRONT canonical stayed at full weight while the rear reference was discounted for being far away — the anchor outvoted the only image showing the back. 0 keeps the old fixed behaviour. Needs a reference at the far views, or nothing holds them together.
object.label: Anchor falloff

object.help: What the anchor decays to 180 degrees away, at falloff 1.0.
object.label: Anchor weight when opposite

object.help: Fraction of sampling the anchor steers for. 1.0 holds identity throughout. Lower it if frames still inherit the anchor's pose after switching transfer to linear.
object.label: Anchor end %

object.help: A look you trained, stacked on top of the pixel LoRA. One style LoRA serves every character, which is why it is the better first thing to train. Watch the total: pixel-art-xl already runs at 1.2, so two style signals compete unless one comes down.
object.label: Style LoRA

object.help: How hard the second style signal pulls. pixel-art-xl already runs at 1.2, so this competes with it: if the look goes muddy, bring one of the two down rather than pushing this up.
object.label: Style LoRA strength

object.help: One character, trained across ALL its views. A LoRA cancels what varies, so pooling the angles teaches it who the character is and discards the camera - which is right, because depth and ControlNet supply the angle. Split per view it would bake the camera into identity and fight them.
object.label: Character LoRA

object.help: Start low (0.4-0.6) and raise. Strength at inference is a reversible dial; an under-trained LoRA is not.
object.label: Character LoRA strength

object.help: Must match the checkpoint's family. A mismatched VAE does not error — it decodes to a colour cast with crushed blacks, which is what an Illustrious A/B produced while borrowing SDXL's.
object.label: VAE

object.help: The Union ProMax model covers openpose, depth, scribble and more in one file, which keeps memory down versus one model per type.
object.label: ControlNet

object.help: The IP-Adapter weights that carry identity from the reference into each frame. It has to match the checkpoint's architecture; an SD1.5 adapter cannot condition an SDXL base.
object.label: IP-Adapter

object.help: Pause after each GPU task so a long queue does not hold the machine at its throttle point all night. Nothing needs the pause to work — it is there because sustained heat shortens a battery and a throttling machine finishes anyway, quietly aged.
object.label: Rest between GPU tasks

object.help: Per rest, and rests fall between tasks — between stages, between candidates, between frames — never before the first or after the last. At 180s a fifty-image night spends two and a half hours resting; that is the trade being made.
object.label: Rest length (seconds)

object.help: Passed to ComfyUI at launch. 'gpu-only' keeps text encoders on the GPU (~8% faster here). 'lowvram' offloads aggressively — slower, but survives bigger models. Requires a restart.
object.label: VRAM policy

object.help: Fraction of unified memory PyTorch may allocate (PYTORCH_MPS_HIGH_WATERMARK_RATIO). 0.0 disables the limit. Lower it to leave room for other apps; too low causes OOM.
object.label: MPS memory ceiling

object.help: Threads for CPU-side tensor work. The M4 has 4 performance and 6 efficiency cores; more threads is not always faster.
object.label: CPU threads (torch)

object.help: Parallel processes for CPU stages such as pixelization. Overrides palette.workers when set.
object.label: CPU worker processes

object.help: Images per queued prompt. Each prompt costs ~35s of fixed overhead regardless of steps, so batching amortises it: batch 4 measured 49s/image versus 71s one at a time.
object.label: Batch size

object.help: Generate a canonical for every view in pose.set instead of one for the first. With a single front anchor the other views must invent their angle - the anchor is the right medium facing the wrong way, the matched reference the right way in the wrong medium. Per view one input is correct on both. They do not drift apart, because each is pinned to a labelled view of the same reference sheet. Costs one generation per view.
object.label: One anchor per view

object.help: One prompt for all candidates instead of one each. Measured 14% faster and under half the swapping — but batching cannot rest between candidates, so an overnight run with cooling on wants this off, and a 1280 canvas may not fit the batch in 16 GB.
object.label: Batch the candidates

object.help: Exemplars carry rendering, not colour. At the 0.35 role default silver-haired exemplars pulled a crimson character toward lavender; 0.18 keeps the brushwork and lets the prompt keep the palette. frames.style_weight was declared and this was not.
object.label: Style exemplar strength

object.help: Which way the anchor faces — a named view or degrees. Blank follows the first entry in pose.set, which is what a sheet wants: every other frame then turns away from it symmetrically.
object.label: Anchor view

object.default: blurry, soft, smooth gradient, antialiased, jpeg artifacts, photo, realistic, 3d render, watermark, signature, text, extra limbs, deformed, low contrast, muddy colors
object.help: Naming a failure is what stops it. The default names the tracing failure (skeleton, bones, stick figure, wireframe).
object.label: Negative prompt

object.help: The Union model handles ten conditioning types and defaults to guessing. Naming the input is the difference between the pose being applied and quietly ignored.
object.label: Anchor control type

object.help: Fraction of sampling before the control begins. At 0 the composition is fixed from the first step; starting late lets the model choose a layout and only then corrects it toward the guide.
object.label: Anchor control start

object.help: Keep equal to canonical.width — the anchor and the frames should be drawn at one scale.
object.label: Width

object.help: Keep equal to canonical.height, for the reason Width is kept equal — the anchor and the frames should be drawn at one scale, or the identity match is comparing different sizes.
object.label: Height

object.help: Identical for every frame on purpose: same seed, same prompt, same anchor, DIFFERENT skeleton is the consistency recipe.
object.label: Seed

object.help: The pixel LoRA's weight on the frames. Keep it equal to canonical.lora_strength: the frames are matched against the anchor, and a different style weight is one more difference that match has to absorb.
object.label: Pixel LoRA strength

object.default: blurry, soft, smooth gradient, antialiased, jpeg artifacts, photo, realistic, 3d render, watermark, signature, text, extra limbs, deformed, low contrast, muddy colors
object.help: The base negative every frame starts from. The pose, backdrop and facing guards append to it rather than replace it, so what you add here survives all of them.
object.label: Negative prompt

object.help: Blank follows the rig's own control channel, which is almost always what you want. Name one only to override, and know that naming the wrong one means the skeleton is quietly ignored rather than refused.
object.label: Pose control type

object.help: Fraction of sampling before the pose control begins. The pose is the whole reason a frame differs from the anchor, so this normally starts at 0 — a late start gives the model time to commit to a pose of its own first.
object.label: ControlNet start %

object.help: Depth is the ONLY channel that carries the viewing angle — a 2D skeleton cannot express yaw. But the capsules are a bare body, so pushing this hard makes a costumed character collapse toward the naked silhouette: at 0.75 a veiled figure came back columnar.
object.label: Depth strength

object.help: When the depth channel joins. Depth is what carries the viewing angle, which a 2D skeleton cannot express, so a late start means the early steps commit to the wrong yaw.
object.label: Depth start %

object.help: Hold it long enough to survive the anchor, which runs to 100%.
object.label: Depth end %

object.help: When identity conditioning joins. Late means the frame's layout is settled before the reference is consulted, which protects the pose at the cost of likeness.
object.label: Identity start %

object.help: When identity conditioning stops. Releasing early lets the last steps sharpen without the reference pulling detail back toward itself; holding to 1.0 keeps the likeness tightest.
object.label: Identity end %

object.help: Blank follows pose.size. Both are control images, so they should match the canvas they steer.
object.label: Depth map size

object.help: Cycles simulated before the first kept frame, so the wobble starts settled instead of springing from rest.
object.label: Preroll cycles

tileset.help: Body plan. Decides joint layout and which ControlNet channel the skeleton can be sent to. Only 'humanoid' has a matching OpenPose model; every other rig uses scribble + depth, and 'blob' uses depth alone.
tileset.label: Creature

tileset.help: Named looks applied beneath this pipeline. A sheet may set prompts, palette, sampler values and exemplar images together, because all of those carry a look. Later sheets win over earlier ones, and the pipeline wins over all of them.
tileset.label: Style sheets

tileset.help: Whether this pipeline uses per-image rig annotations. 'skip' ignores them, which is the right default for unattended runs. 'if_present' uses any that exist. 'require' holds the job until every reference has one, for when you intend to mark them by hand before a long batch.
tileset.label: Reference annotation

tileset.help: Used for the output folder name.
tileset.label: Run name

tileset.help: The character. Read by every stage that writes a prompt, so it lives in one place.
tileset.label: Subject

tileset.help: Appended to the subject. 'plain flat background' makes the background keying in the palette stage much cleaner.
tileset.label: Style

tileset.help: Stop the run after this stage so its output can be reviewed or edited before the expensive stages consume it. Stopping after 'pose' is what makes the rig editor useful — resume continues with whatever you saved.
tileset.label: Pause after stage

tileset.help: Validated before anything runs: a stage whose inputs aren't produced earlier is rejected with an explanation. Consecutive independent CPU stages run in parallel; GPU stages never do.
tileset.label: Stage order

tileset.help: 'library' uses hand-authored poses (best quality). 'llm' drafts a new action from text and caches it. 'tpose' synthesises the rig's reference pose — what a character sheet uses. 'annotation' takes the pose from a reference image you marked up: the joints you placed become the control image, so the generation reproduces that composition with your character in it. Mark one up in the Run tab under 'Annotate reference'.
tileset.label: Pose source

tileset.help: Poses are stored in body space and projected here, so one pose file serves every camera. Accepts a raw angle too (e.g. 160). Past ~100 degrees the face keypoints drop automatically, which is how the skeleton tells ControlNet the character faces away.
tileset.label: Viewing angle

tileset.help: Blank uses every frame in the pose file.
tileset.label: Frame count

tileset.help: Fraction of the canvas the figure occupies. 0 leaves the pose at the size the rig was authored at, which is small — the humanoid spans 68%, so a third of the generation resolution goes to empty background. 0.88 makes a 128px sprite's character 113 pixels tall instead of 87, for the same GPU time. The tightest axis decides, so a wingspan cannot run off the sides.
tileset.label: Frame fill

tileset.help: Should match the generation resolution.
tileset.label: Skeleton size

tileset.help: Scales forward/back motion without re-authoring the pose. Above 1.0 makes a swing reach further.
tileset.label: Depth exaggeration

tileset.help: Scales the character's left/right spread.
tileset.label: Stance width

tileset.help: Grey value for the part of the body closest to the camera. 255 is the convention the ControlNet was trained on.
tileset.label: Nearest brightness

tileset.help: Grey value for the farthest part. Raising it flattens the map, which weakens the sense of rotation; lowering it past ~40 starts losing the far limb into the background.
tileset.label: Farthest brightness

tileset.help: How heavy the creature is, as distinct from how tall. The depth capsules hang off the bones, and their radius is the only thing that says a character is broad — proportions make a figure taller, this makes the same skeleton read as heavyset. A YAML mapping works too, for a pot-bellied build with thin arms: {torso: 1.6, arms: 0.9}, using the same group names as proportions.
tileset.label: Build (bulk)

tileset.help: Gaussian radius over the rendered limbs. Some blur is wanted: a hard-edged depth map reads as geometry and the model draws tubes.
tileset.label: Softness

tileset.help: PIN THIS. Every frame reuses it; changing it changes the character entirely.
tileset.label: Seed

tileset.help: Off for the canonical. LCM is ~3x faster but drops prompt details — it lost 'holding a sword' in testing.
tileset.label: Fast LCM mode

tileset.help: 25 for quality. Below ~8 you pay fixed overhead for worse output.
tileset.label: Steps

tileset.help: Prompt adherence. 7 is the SDXL sweet spot; use 1.5 with LCM.
tileset.label: CFG

tileset.help: 1.2 is the pixel-art-xl author's recommendation.
tileset.label: Pixel LoRA strength

tileset.help: SDXL is trained at 1024; smaller degrades quality and saves less time than you'd expect.
tileset.label: Width

tileset.help: Pairs with Width. SDXL is trained at 1024x1024 and the further the canvas is from square, the more the composition drifts from what the prompt asked for.
tileset.label: Height

tileset.help: On for drafts, off for the final render.
tileset.label: Fast LCM mode

tileset.help: Frames are conditioned on the anchor, so they need fewer steps than it does. With Fast LCM mode on this wants single digits — LCM is distilled to converge in a handful and the rest buy nothing. With it off, match canonical.steps.
tileset.label: Steps

tileset.help: 1.5 with LCM. Using 7 with LCM burns the image.
tileset.label: CFG

tileset.help: 1.0 generates fresh. Below 1.0 carries over the input latent — this is the 'how much of the previous step survives' dial.
tileset.label: Denoise

tileset.help: Add face, eyes, nose to the NEGATIVE on rear and near-rear frames. Depth renders the head as a capsule - measured, a front and rear depth map differ ~6% across the head and the two side maps are identical under mirroring - and the skeleton channel, which does encode facing, is off for a standing sheet. So nothing geometric says 'no face' and the model draws one.
tileset.label: Guard against faces on rear views

tileset.help: Appends anti-skeleton terms to the negative prompt whenever a pose guide is used. Without it the model sometimes draws the guide itself — measured: a T-pose produced a figure with swords where its arms should be, and an undead-looking body.
tileset.label: Guard against tracing

tileset.help: Off is right for a standing character sheet. Measured: with it on, legs came back as white shafts with ball joints — the guide drawn as bones — while depth alone gave armoured legs and boots. Leave it on for attack, hit and fall, where the pose is the point.
tileset.label: Use the pose guide

tileset.help: How hard the pose guide is enforced. Above ~0.85 the model starts tracing the guide instead of using it, which is what produces stick-figure or skeletal output.
tileset.label: ControlNet strength

tileset.help: Fraction of sampling the guide steers for. 0.55 lands the pose and leaves the second half for the LoRA to render a character over it; holding it longer produces a traced stick figure.
tileset.label: ControlNet end %

tileset.help: 0.3-0.5 style nudge | 0.6 mixed | 0.8-1.0 identity lock. Too high looks pasted on and fights the pose.
tileset.label: IP-Adapter weight

tileset.help: How the reference is blended into conditioning.
tileset.label: Weight type

tileset.help: 'extract' derives from the canonical and always matches the art. 'file' reuses a committed palette, keeping separate runs of the same character on-model. 'llm' chooses one by subject — only chooses; applying it stays deterministic, which is what stops frames drifting in colour.
tileset.label: Palette source

tileset.help: One of the .hex files under palettes/. Committing one is what makes colour exact rather than probabilistic: snapping is deterministic, so two runs of the same character land on the same entries.
tileset.label: Palette file

tileset.help: Number of colours the whole animation is quantised to.
tileset.label: Palette size

tileset.help: 8 gives 128px sprites from 1024. Verified as this LoRA's true pixel grid by an intra-block variance sweep.
tileset.label: Downscale factor

tileset.help: median measured 100% structural accuracy against ground truth; mode only 70% (noise makes every colour unique). 'clipped' means the block after throwing out pixels further than the tolerance from its mean, then re-averaging - it rejects a specular outlier that would drag a plain mean, while still letting the survivors average rather than picking one of them.
tileset.label: Block reduction

tileset.help: RGB distance from the block mean beyond which a pixel is discarded before re-averaging. Fixed rather than a multiple of the block's own spread, so one setting behaves the same on a flat block and a busy one. Blocks where too little survives fall back to median, which is what stops thin outlines being eaten.
tileset.label: Clip tolerance

tileset.help: Edge-connected background within this tolerance becomes transparent. Enclosed regions are preserved.
tileset.label: Background tolerance

tileset.help: Nearest-neighbour, for viewing.
tileset.label: Frame upscale

tileset.help: Blank uses one per core. Frames are independent.
tileset.label: Worker processes

tileset.help: Named in the prompt and removed by the keyer, so the two agree. Asking for a 'plain' background gets a lit studio card with a cast shadow, because that is what the words describe. Magenta rather than chroma green: green sits close to skin and cloth tones, and every pixel it bleeds into is one the palette has to spend an entry on.
tileset.label: Backdrop colour

tileset.help: Off leaves the background to the prompt, which is what you want if a scene is part of the art.
tileset.label: Force a backdrop

tileset.help: How 'nearest colour' is decided when snapping to a fixed palette. 'weighted' applies luminance weights and costs nothing over plain RGB. 'luma' matches brightness first and is the one built for sprites — a sprite reads by its value structure, so an entry of the wrong lightness collapses the form even when the hue is right. 'lab' is perceptually uniform and the most faithful for recolouring, at roughly ten times the cost. 'rgb' is what earlier outputs used. Irrelevant when the palette is extracted, since it already came from these pixels.
tileset.label: Colour matching

tileset.help: Trades flat blocks for apparent colour depth. Leave off for the chunky RPG-Maker idiom; turn on when a small palette has to carry a gradient.
tileset.label: Dither

tileset.help: Blank puts every frame in one row.
tileset.label: Sheet columns

tileset.help: Nearest-neighbour magnification baked into the written sheet, so 4x is sixteen times the pixels on disk. Leave it at 1 unless the file has to arrive somewhere that will not magnify it itself — the editor scales in the browser and stays sharp at any zoom.
tileset.label: Sheet upscale

tileset.help: Where ComfyUI is listening, normally http://127.0.0.1:8188. Set it here only to point one config at a different instance than the machine default in _global.yaml.
tileset.label: ComfyUI host

tileset.label: Arm length

tileset.help: Below 1.0 gives a stubby, chibi stance.
tileset.label: Leg length

tileset.help: Ignored by rigs with no tail.
tileset.label: Tail length

tileset.help: Ignored by rigs with no wings.
tileset.label: Wing span

tileset.help: Octopoid rigs only.
tileset.label: Tentacle length

tileset.help: Serpent and centipede rigs only.
tileset.label: Segment length

tileset.help: Off by default for a character sheet, on for an animation, and the same prop list serves both. A sheet is a reference document - a weapon occludes the torso and arm it crosses, and is a long rigid volume the model will trace instead of the limb behind it. An attack animation is the opposite: without the weapon the arm swings at nothing.
tileset.label: Draw held objects

tileset.help: Base diffusion weights. SDXL is what the pixel LoRA was trained against; swapping the base usually means swapping the LoRA too.
tileset.label: Checkpoint

tileset.help: The LoRA that makes the output read as pixel art rather than a downscaled painting. Every other default here is tuned around it, so swapping it means re-tuning both lora_strength dials.
tileset.label: Style LoRA

tileset.help: Apply the canonical sprite to every frame at equal weight, underneath the matched identity reference. It is the only input that does not vary, so it is what keeps frames on-model with each other. Turning it off reverts to steering from the reference alone, which leaves rear views with no anchor.
tileset.label: Anchor to canonical

tileset.help: How hard the canonical pulls. Too high and every frame becomes the canonical's pose; too low and the frames drift apart.
tileset.label: Anchor weight

tileset.help: What the anchor carries. Keep 'linear'. 'style and composition' also copies the canonical's LAYOUT, and the canonical is front-facing — at anchor weight 0.9 it outvoted the depth map that carries yaw and every side and rear frame came back facing front, with the canonical's backdrop over the keyed one.
tileset.label: Anchor transfer

tileset.help: How much the anchor weakens as a frame turns away from it. Reference weight already falls off with angle; the anchor's did not, so on a rear frame the FRONT canonical stayed at full weight while the rear reference was discounted for being far away — the anchor outvoted the only image showing the back. 0 keeps the old fixed behaviour. Needs a reference at the far views, or nothing holds them together.
tileset.label: Anchor falloff

tileset.help: What the anchor decays to 180 degrees away, at falloff 1.0.
tileset.label: Anchor weight when opposite

tileset.help: Fraction of sampling the anchor steers for. 1.0 holds identity throughout. Lower it if frames still inherit the anchor's pose after switching transfer to linear.
tileset.label: Anchor end %

tileset.help: A look you trained, stacked on top of the pixel LoRA. One style LoRA serves every character, which is why it is the better first thing to train. Watch the total: pixel-art-xl already runs at 1.2, so two style signals compete unless one comes down.
tileset.label: Style LoRA

tileset.help: How hard the second style signal pulls. pixel-art-xl already runs at 1.2, so this competes with it: if the look goes muddy, bring one of the two down rather than pushing this up.
tileset.label: Style LoRA strength

tileset.help: One character, trained across ALL its views. A LoRA cancels what varies, so pooling the angles teaches it who the character is and discards the camera - which is right, because depth and ControlNet supply the angle. Split per view it would bake the camera into identity and fight them.
tileset.label: Character LoRA

tileset.help: Start low (0.4-0.6) and raise. Strength at inference is a reversible dial; an under-trained LoRA is not.
tileset.label: Character LoRA strength

tileset.help: Must match the checkpoint's family. A mismatched VAE does not error — it decodes to a colour cast with crushed blacks, which is what an Illustrious A/B produced while borrowing SDXL's.
tileset.label: VAE

tileset.help: The Union ProMax model covers openpose, depth, scribble and more in one file, which keeps memory down versus one model per type.
tileset.label: ControlNet

tileset.help: The IP-Adapter weights that carry identity from the reference into each frame. It has to match the checkpoint's architecture; an SD1.5 adapter cannot condition an SDXL base.
tileset.label: IP-Adapter

tileset.help: Pause after each GPU task so a long queue does not hold the machine at its throttle point all night. Nothing needs the pause to work — it is there because sustained heat shortens a battery and a throttling machine finishes anyway, quietly aged.
tileset.label: Rest between GPU tasks

tileset.help: Per rest, and rests fall between tasks — between stages, between candidates, between frames — never before the first or after the last. At 180s a fifty-image night spends two and a half hours resting; that is the trade being made.
tileset.label: Rest length (seconds)

tileset.help: Passed to ComfyUI at launch. 'gpu-only' keeps text encoders on the GPU (~8% faster here). 'lowvram' offloads aggressively — slower, but survives bigger models. Requires a restart.
tileset.label: VRAM policy

tileset.help: Fraction of unified memory PyTorch may allocate (PYTORCH_MPS_HIGH_WATERMARK_RATIO). 0.0 disables the limit. Lower it to leave room for other apps; too low causes OOM.
tileset.label: MPS memory ceiling

tileset.help: Threads for CPU-side tensor work. The M4 has 4 performance and 6 efficiency cores; more threads is not always faster.
tileset.label: CPU threads (torch)

tileset.help: Parallel processes for CPU stages such as pixelization. Overrides palette.workers when set.
tileset.label: CPU worker processes

tileset.help: Images per queued prompt. Each prompt costs ~35s of fixed overhead regardless of steps, so batching amortises it: batch 4 measured 49s/image versus 71s one at a time.
tileset.label: Batch size

tileset.help: Generate a canonical for every view in pose.set instead of one for the first. With a single front anchor the other views must invent their angle - the anchor is the right medium facing the wrong way, the matched reference the right way in the wrong medium. Per view one input is correct on both. They do not drift apart, because each is pinned to a labelled view of the same reference sheet. Costs one generation per view.
tileset.label: One anchor per view

tileset.help: One prompt for all candidates instead of one each. Measured 14% faster and under half the swapping — but batching cannot rest between candidates, so an overnight run with cooling on wants this off, and a 1280 canvas may not fit the batch in 16 GB.
tileset.label: Batch the candidates

tileset.help: Exemplars carry rendering, not colour. At the 0.35 role default silver-haired exemplars pulled a crimson character toward lavender; 0.18 keeps the brushwork and lets the prompt keep the palette. frames.style_weight was declared and this was not.
tileset.label: Style exemplar strength

tileset.help: Which way the anchor faces — a named view or degrees. Blank follows the first entry in pose.set, which is what a sheet wants: every other frame then turns away from it symmetrically.
tileset.label: Anchor view

tileset.default: blurry, soft, smooth gradient, antialiased, jpeg artifacts, photo, realistic, 3d render, watermark, signature, text, extra limbs, deformed, low contrast, muddy colors
tileset.help: Naming a failure is what stops it. The default names the tracing failure (skeleton, bones, stick figure, wireframe).
tileset.label: Negative prompt

tileset.help: The Union model handles ten conditioning types and defaults to guessing. Naming the input is the difference between the pose being applied and quietly ignored.
tileset.label: Anchor control type

tileset.help: Fraction of sampling before the control begins. At 0 the composition is fixed from the first step; starting late lets the model choose a layout and only then corrects it toward the guide.
tileset.label: Anchor control start

tileset.help: Keep equal to canonical.width — the anchor and the frames should be drawn at one scale.
tileset.label: Width

tileset.help: Keep equal to canonical.height, for the reason Width is kept equal — the anchor and the frames should be drawn at one scale, or the identity match is comparing different sizes.
tileset.label: Height

tileset.help: Identical for every frame on purpose: same seed, same prompt, same anchor, DIFFERENT skeleton is the consistency recipe.
tileset.label: Seed

tileset.help: The pixel LoRA's weight on the frames. Keep it equal to canonical.lora_strength: the frames are matched against the anchor, and a different style weight is one more difference that match has to absorb.
tileset.label: Pixel LoRA strength

tileset.default: blurry, soft, smooth gradient, antialiased, jpeg artifacts, photo, realistic, 3d render, watermark, signature, text, extra limbs, deformed, low contrast, muddy colors
tileset.help: The base negative every frame starts from. The pose, backdrop and facing guards append to it rather than replace it, so what you add here survives all of them.
tileset.label: Negative prompt

tileset.help: Blank follows the rig's own control channel, which is almost always what you want. Name one only to override, and know that naming the wrong one means the skeleton is quietly ignored rather than refused.
tileset.label: Pose control type

tileset.help: Fraction of sampling before the pose control begins. The pose is the whole reason a frame differs from the anchor, so this normally starts at 0 — a late start gives the model time to commit to a pose of its own first.
tileset.label: ControlNet start %

tileset.help: Depth is the ONLY channel that carries the viewing angle — a 2D skeleton cannot express yaw. But the capsules are a bare body, so pushing this hard makes a costumed character collapse toward the naked silhouette: at 0.75 a veiled figure came back columnar.
tileset.label: Depth strength

tileset.help: When the depth channel joins. Depth is what carries the viewing angle, which a 2D skeleton cannot express, so a late start means the early steps commit to the wrong yaw.
tileset.label: Depth start %

tileset.help: Hold it long enough to survive the anchor, which runs to 100%.
tileset.label: Depth end %

tileset.help: When identity conditioning joins. Late means the frame's layout is settled before the reference is consulted, which protects the pose at the cost of likeness.
tileset.label: Identity start %

tileset.help: When identity conditioning stops. Releasing early lets the last steps sharpen without the reference pulling detail back toward itself; holding to 1.0 keeps the likeness tightest.
tileset.label: Identity end %

tileset.help: Blank follows pose.size. Both are control images, so they should match the canvas they steer.
tileset.label: Depth map size

tileset.help: Cycles simulated before the first kept frame, so the wobble starts settled instead of springing from rest.
tileset.label: Preroll cycles
